Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information._(January 2013)_
[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Patricia_2015-10-23_1730Z.jpg/250px-Patricia_2015-10-23_1730Z.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Patricia_2015-10-23_1730Z.jpg)

[Hurricane Patricia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Patricia "Hurricane Patricia") shortly after reaching its record peak intensity on October 23, 2015, while approaching Western Mexico

This is a **list of notable Pacific hurricanes**, subdivided by reason for notability. Notability means that it has met some criterion or achieved some statistic, or is part of a top ten for some superlative. It includes lists and rankings of [Pacific hurricanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_hurricane "Pacific hurricane") by different characteristics and impacts.

Characteristics include extremes of location, such as the northernmost or most equator-ward formation or position of a tropical cyclone. Other characteristics include its central pressure, windspeed, category on the [Saffir–Simpson scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saffir%E2%80%93Simpson_scale "Saffir–Simpson scale"), [cyclogenesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclogenesis "Tropical cyclogenesis") outside of a normal [hurricane season's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_hurricane "Pacific hurricane") timeframe, or storms that remain unnamed despite forming after tropical cyclone naming began in 1960. Another characteristic is how long a system lasted from formation to dissipation. These include the cost of damage, the number of casualties, as well as meteorological statistics such as rainfall point maximum, wind speed, and minimum pressure.

## Impact

### Retired names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Retired names")]

Main article: [List of retired Pacific hurricane names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_retired_Pacific_hurricane_names "List of retired Pacific hurricane names")

The following names have been retired in the East Pacific (in chronological order): [Hazel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Hazel_(1965) "Tropical Storm Hazel (1965)"), [Adele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Adele_(1970) "Hurricane Adele (1970)"), [Fico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fico "Hurricane Fico"), [Knut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Knut_(1987) "Tropical Storm Knut (1987)"), [Iva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iva_(1988) "Hurricane Iva (1988)"), [Fefa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fefa "Hurricane Fefa"), [Ismael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ismael "Hurricane Ismael"), [Pauline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Pauline "Hurricane Pauline"), [Adolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Adolph_(2001) "Hurricane Adolph (2001)"), Israel, [Kenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Kenna "Hurricane Kenna"), [Alma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Alma "Tropical Storm Alma"), [Manuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Manuel "Hurricane Manuel"), [Odile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Odile "Hurricane Odile"), Isis, [Patricia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Patricia "Hurricane Patricia"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HRD-1)[Dora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Dora_(2023) "Hurricane Dora (2023)"), [Otis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Otis "Hurricane Otis"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-WMO24-2) and [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_John_(2024) "Hurricane John (2024)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-WMO25-3)

In addition, the following names have been retired in the Central Pacific (in chronological order): [Iwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iwa "Hurricane Iwa"), [Iniki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iniki "Hurricane Iniki"), [Paka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoon_Paka "Typhoon Paka"), and [Ioke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ioke "Hurricane Ioke").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HRD-1)

From the lists above, the names Hazel and Adele were retired for unclear reasons.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HazelAdeleRetirement-4) Also, the names Adolph, Israel, and Isis were retired because of political considerations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HRD-1) In particular, the name Isis was pre-emptively removed in 2015 from the list of names for 2016 after being deemed inappropriate because of the [eponymous militant group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-retired-5)

### Naming history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Naming history")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Oho_2015-10-06_2310Z.jpg/250px-Oho_2015-10-06_2310Z.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oho_2015-10-06_2310Z.jpg)

[Hurricane Oho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Oho "Hurricane Oho"), the eighth system to receive a central Pacific name in 2015

Naming of tropical cyclones in the eastern north Pacific began in the [1960 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Pacific_hurricane_season "1960 Pacific hurricane season"). That year, four lists of names were created. The plan was to proceed in a manner similar to that of the western Pacific; that is, the name of the first storm in one season would be the next unused one from the same list, and when the bottom of one list was reached the next list was started. This scheme was abandoned in 1965 and next year, the lists started being recycled on a four-year rotation, starting with the A name each year.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-ATWC-51) That same general scheme remains in use today, although the names and lists are different. On average, the eastern north Pacific sees about sixteen named storms per year.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-NCDC_2006_summary-52)

## Duration records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Duration records")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Tina_1992-09-30_1801Z.png/250px-Tina_1992-09-30_1801Z.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tina_1992-09-30_1801Z.png)

[Hurricane Tina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Tina_(1992) "Hurricane Tina (1992)"), the longest-lasting Pacific hurricane east of the International Date Line

This lists all Pacific hurricanes that existed as tropical cyclones while in the Pacific Ocean east of [the dateline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/180th_meridian "180th meridian") for more than two weeks continuously. Hurricanes John and Dora spent some time in the west Pacific before dissipating. John spent eleven days west of the dateline; if that time was included John would have existed for a total of 30 days and 18 hours, while including Dora's time in the west Pacific would mean that it existed for 18 days.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53) One Atlantic hurricane, [Hurricane Joan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Joan%E2%80%93Miriam "Hurricane Joan–Miriam"), crossed into this basin and was renamed Miriam,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-E15-69) giving it a total lifespan of 22 days,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HURDAT-70) but not all of that was in the Pacific. 1993's Greg formed from the remnants of [Tropical Storm Bret (1993)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Bret_(1993) "Tropical Storm Bret (1993)").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-E15-69) Its time as an Atlantic system is excluded.

All of these systems except Trudy, Olaf, Connie and Lala existed in both the east and central Pacific, and all except Olaf were hurricanes. Hurricane Trudy of 1990 is thus the longest lived eastern Pacific hurricane to stay in the eastern Pacific. Tropical Storm Olaf of 1997 is hence the longest-lived eastern Pacific tropical cyclone _not_ to reach hurricane intensity.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53)

Prior to [Hurricane Lala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Lala "Hurricane Lala")[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_], no known tropical cyclone forming in the central north Pacific lasted for longer than 14 days without crossing into [another basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_basins "Tropical cyclone basins").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53) The pre-2026 tropical cyclone that formed in the central Pacific and spent the most time there was [Hurricane Ana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ana "Hurricane Ana"), at 12.75 days from formation to extratropical transition.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-AnaTCR-71)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-tc_records_CPHC-72)

It used to be that when a Pacific named storm crossed North America and made it to the Atlantic (or vice versa), it would receive the next name on the respective basin's list. However, in 2000 this policy was changed so that a tropical cyclone will keep its name if it remains a tropical cyclone during the entire passage. Only if it dissipates and then re-forms does it get renamed.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-b5-87)

It eventually developed an [eye-like](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_(cyclone) "Eye (cyclone)") structure.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-NASA-91C-113) Its track data indicates that it crossed from the central to the east Pacific because it formed at longitude 149°W and dissipated at 135°W.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Padgett_tracks-114)[NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA"), which is not a meteorological organization, called this system a [subtropical cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_cyclone "Subtropical cyclone"), and the Naval Research Laboratory Monterey had enough interest in it to call it 91C.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-NASA-91C-113) The system has also been called [extratropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extratropical_cyclone "Extratropical cyclone").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CHC-115) This cyclone is unofficial because it is not included in the seasonal reports of either [Regional Specialized Meteorological Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Specialized_Meteorological_Center "Regional Specialized Meteorological Center").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CPHC_2006-116)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-NHC_2006_archive-117)

## Unusual landfall locations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Unusual landfall locations")]

### California

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: California")]

See also: [List of California hurricanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_California_hurricanes "List of California hurricanes")

*   **After October or before June, 1854**– A system considered a tropical cyclone makes landfall just north of the [Golden Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate "Golden Gate").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Visher_p296-88)
*   **October 2, 1858**– A [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1858_San_Diego_hurricane "1858 San Diego hurricane") makes a direct hit on Southern California before dissipating. The hurricane may or may not have made landfall in [San Diego County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_County,_California "San Diego County, California"), due to uncertainty in the track reconstruction. [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego") experienced hurricane-force winds, with torrential rainfall recorded all across Southern California.
*   **After October or before June, 1859**– A system considered a tropical cyclone makes landfall between [Cape Mendocino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Mendocino "Cape Mendocino") and [San Francisco Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay "San Francisco Bay").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Visher_p296-88)
*   **September 25, 1939**– The [1939 California tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_California_tropical_storm "1939 California tropical storm") makes landfall in [San Pedro, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Pedro,_California "San Pedro, California"), killing 45[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Hurd_1939-124) to 93 people.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-history_of_sig_events_p14-125)
*   **September 6, 1972**– [Tropical Depression Hyacinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Pacific_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Hyacinth "1972 Pacific hurricane season") makes landfall.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_Hyacinth_1972-126)
*   **September 6, 1978**– [Tropical Depression Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Norman_(1978) "Hurricane Norman (1978)") makes landfall.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_Norman_1978-127)

*   **August 7, 1958**– A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1958_Pacific_hurricane_season#Tropical_Storm_Seven "1958 Pacific hurricane season") makes landfall on the [Big Island of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Island_of_Hawaii "Big Island of Hawaii").[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_7_1958-128)
*   **August 7, 1959**– [Hurricane Dot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Dot_(1959) "Hurricane Dot (1959)") makes landfall on [Kauai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kauai "Kauai").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_DOT_1959-129)
*   **October 20, 1983**– [Tropical Depression Raymond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_Pacific_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Raymond "1983 Pacific hurricane season") makes landfall on [Molokai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molokai "Molokai"), [Oahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oahu "Oahu"), and [Kauai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kauai "Kauai").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_RAYMOND_1983-130)
*   **August 3, 1988**– [Tropical Depression Gilma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Pacific_hurricane_season#Tropical_Storm_Gilma "1988 Pacific hurricane season") makes landfall on Maui and [Molokai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molokai "Molokai").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_GILMA_1988-131)
*   **September 11, 1992**– [Hurricane Iniki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iniki "Hurricane Iniki") makes landfall on [Kauai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kauai "Kauai"), killing six throughout the islands.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CPHC_1992-64)
*   **September 14, 1992**– [Tropical Depression Orlene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Pacific_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Orlene "1992 Pacific hurricane season") makes landfall on the Big Island.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CPHC_1992-64)
*   **July 24, 1993**– [Tropical Depression Eugene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Eugene_(1993) "Hurricane Eugene (1993)") makes landfall on the [Big Island of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Island_of_Hawaii "Big Island of Hawaii").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_EUGENE_1993-132)
*   **August 8, 2014**– [Tropical Storm Iselle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iselle_(2014) "Hurricane Iselle (2014)") makes landfall on the [Big Island of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Island_of_Hawaii "Big Island of Hawaii"), killing one on [Kauai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kauai "Kauai").[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Fox_News-133)
*   **July 24, 2016**– [Tropical Storm Darby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Darby_(2016) "Hurricane Darby (2016)") makes landfall on the [Big Island of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Island_of_Hawaii "Big Island of Hawaii").[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Al_Jazeera-134)
*   **September 12, 2018**– [Tropical Storm Olivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Olivia_(2018) "Hurricane Olivia (2018)") makes landfall on [Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui "Maui") and [Lanai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanai "Lanai").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CNN-135)

[Hurricane Patricia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Patricia "Hurricane Patricia") shortly after reaching its record peak intensity on October 23, 2015, while approaching Western Mexico

This is a **list of notable Pacific hurricanes**, subdivided by reason for notability. Notability means that it has met some criterion or achieved some statistic, or is part of a top ten for some superlative. It includes lists and rankings of [Pacific hurricanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_hurricane "Pacific hurricane") by different characteristics and impacts.

Characteristics include extremes of location, such as the northernmost or most equator-ward formation or position of a tropical cyclone. Other characteristics include its central pressure, windspeed, category on the [Saffir–Simpson scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saffir%E2%80%93Simpson_scale "Saffir–Simpson scale"), [cyclogenesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclogenesis "Tropical cyclogenesis") outside of a normal [hurricane season's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_hurricane "Pacific hurricane") timeframe, or storms that remain unnamed despite forming after tropical cyclone naming began in 1960. Another characteristic is how long a system lasted from formation to dissipation. These include the cost of damage, the number of casualties, as well as meteorological statistics such as rainfall point maximum, wind speed, and minimum pressure.

### Retired names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Retired names")]

Main article: [List of retired Pacific hurricane names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_retired_Pacific_hurricane_names "List of retired Pacific hurricane names")

The following names have been retired in the East Pacific (in chronological order): [Hazel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Hazel_(1965) "Tropical Storm Hazel (1965)"), [Adele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Adele_(1970) "Hurricane Adele (1970)"), [Fico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fico "Hurricane Fico"), [Knut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Knut_(1987) "Tropical Storm Knut (1987)"), [Iva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iva_(1988) "Hurricane Iva (1988)"), [Fefa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fefa "Hurricane Fefa"), [Ismael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ismael "Hurricane Ismael"), [Pauline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Pauline "Hurricane Pauline"), [Adolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Adolph_(2001) "Hurricane Adolph (2001)"), Israel, [Kenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Kenna "Hurricane Kenna"), [Alma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Alma "Tropical Storm Alma"), [Manuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Manuel "Hurricane Manuel"), [Odile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Odile "Hurricane Odile"), Isis, [Patricia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Patricia "Hurricane Patricia"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HRD-1)[Dora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Dora_(2023) "Hurricane Dora (2023)"), [Otis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Otis "Hurricane Otis"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-WMO24-2) and [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_John_(2024) "Hurricane John (2024)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-WMO25-3)

In addition, the following names have been retired in the Central Pacific (in chronological order): [Iwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iwa "Hurricane Iwa"), [Iniki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iniki "Hurricane Iniki"), [Paka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoon_Paka "Typhoon Paka"), and [Ioke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ioke "Hurricane Ioke").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HRD-1)

From the lists above, the names Hazel and Adele were retired for unclear reasons.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HazelAdeleRetirement-4) Also, the names Adolph, Israel, and Isis were retired because of political considerations.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HRD-1) In particular, the name Isis was pre-emptively removed in 2015 from the list of names for 2016 after being deemed inappropriate because of the [eponymous militant group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-retired-5)

## Seasonal activity and records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Seasonal activity and records")]

A season without cyclones has happened a few times since 1966, most recently in [1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Pacific_hurricane_season "1979 Pacific hurricane season").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CPHC_all-42)

Before 1971 and especially 1966, data in this basin is extremely unreliable. The geostationary satellite era began in 1966,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Rhome_Brown_Mainelli_Blake-43) and that year is often considered the first year of reliable tropical records.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Padgett_August_2000-44) Intensity estimates are most reliable starting in the 1971 season. A few years later, the [Dvorak technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvorak_technique "Dvorak technique") came into use. Those two factors make intensity estimates more reliable starting in that year.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Padgett_August_2000-44) For these reasons, seasons prior to 1971 are not included.

### Naming history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Naming history")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Oho_2015-10-06_2310Z.jpg/250px-Oho_2015-10-06_2310Z.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oho_2015-10-06_2310Z.jpg)

[Hurricane Oho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Oho "Hurricane Oho"), the eighth system to receive a central Pacific name in 2015

Naming of tropical cyclones in the eastern north Pacific began in the [1960 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Pacific_hurricane_season "1960 Pacific hurricane season"). That year, four lists of names were created. The plan was to proceed in a manner similar to that of the western Pacific; that is, the name of the first storm in one season would be the next unused one from the same list, and when the bottom of one list was reached the next list was started. This scheme was abandoned in 1965 and next year, the lists started being recycled on a four-year rotation, starting with the A name each year.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-ATWC-51) That same general scheme remains in use today, although the names and lists are different. On average, the eastern north Pacific sees about sixteen named storms per year.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-NCDC_2006_summary-52)

Four of the July [cyclones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclone "Cyclone") during the 2016 season

Specific seasonal data in the Eastern Pacific basin was first compiled in 1949.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53) Therefore, seasons before 1949 are excluded from the "Most named" column.

Also, before 1971 and especially 1966, data in this basin is extremely unreliable. The geostationary satellite era began in 1966,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Rhome_Brown_Mainelli_Blake-43) and that year is often considered the first year of reliable tropical records.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Padgett_August_2000-44) Intensity estimates are more reliable starting in the 1971 season. A few years later, the [Dvorak technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvorak_technique "Dvorak technique") came into use. Those two make intensity estimates more reliable starting in that year.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Padgett_August_2000-44) For these reasons, seasons before 1971 are not included in the "Fewest named" column.

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Tina_1992-09-30_1801Z.png/250px-Tina_1992-09-30_1801Z.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tina_1992-09-30_1801Z.png)

[Hurricane Tina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Tina_(1992) "Hurricane Tina (1992)"), the longest-lasting Pacific hurricane east of the International Date Line

This lists all Pacific hurricanes that existed as tropical cyclones while in the Pacific Ocean east of [the dateline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/180th_meridian "180th meridian") for more than two weeks continuously. Hurricanes John and Dora spent some time in the west Pacific before dissipating. John spent eleven days west of the dateline; if that time was included John would have existed for a total of 30 days and 18 hours, while including Dora's time in the west Pacific would mean that it existed for 18 days.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53) One Atlantic hurricane, [Hurricane Joan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Joan%E2%80%93Miriam "Hurricane Joan–Miriam"), crossed into this basin and was renamed Miriam,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-E15-69) giving it a total lifespan of 22 days,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HURDAT-70) but not all of that was in the Pacific. 1993's Greg formed from the remnants of [Tropical Storm Bret (1993)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Bret_(1993) "Tropical Storm Bret (1993)").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-E15-69) Its time as an Atlantic system is excluded.

All of these systems except Trudy, Olaf, Connie and Lala existed in both the east and central Pacific, and all except Olaf were hurricanes. Hurricane Trudy of 1990 is thus the longest lived eastern Pacific hurricane to stay in the eastern Pacific. Tropical Storm Olaf of 1997 is hence the longest-lived eastern Pacific tropical cyclone _not_ to reach hurricane intensity.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53)

Prior to [Hurricane Lala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Lala "Hurricane Lala")[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_], no known tropical cyclone forming in the central north Pacific lasted for longer than 14 days without crossing into [another basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_basins "Tropical cyclone basins").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53) The pre-2026 tropical cyclone that formed in the central Pacific and spent the most time there was [Hurricane Ana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ana "Hurricane Ana"), at 12.75 days from formation to extratropical transition.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-AnaTCR-71)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-tc_records_CPHC-72)

It used to be that when a Pacific named storm crossed North America and made it to the Atlantic (or vice versa), it would receive the next name on the respective basin's list. However, in 2000 this policy was changed so that a tropical cyclone will keep its name if it remains a tropical cyclone during the entire passage. Only if it dissipates and then re-forms does it get renamed.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-b5-87)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Tracks_of_Central-East_Pacific_crossover_storms.png/250px-Tracks_of_Central-East_Pacific_crossover_storms.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tracks_of_Central-East_Pacific_crossover_storms.png)

Tracks of tropical cyclones that crossed from the central Pacific to the eastern Pacific

Tropical cyclones crossing from the eastern Pacific to the central Pacific are routine; ones going the other way are not. That event has happened four times.

| Season | Name | Ref. |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [1975](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_Pacific_hurricane_season "1975 Pacific hurricane season") | [Unnamed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_Pacific_Northwest_hurricane "1975 Pacific Northwest hurricane") | [[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53) |
| [1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Pacific_hurricane_season "1982 Pacific hurricane season") | [Ema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Ema_(1982) "Tropical Storm Ema (1982)") | [[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53) |
| [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Pacific_hurricane_season "2015 Pacific hurricane season") | [Olaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Olaf_(2015) "Hurricane Olaf (2015)")† | [[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-111) |
| [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Pacific_hurricane_season "2016 Pacific hurricane season") | [Ulika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ulika_(2016) "Hurricane Ulika (2016)")† | [[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-112) |

† System crossed 140°W more than once.

In addition to these, an [unofficial cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Central_Pacific_cyclone "2006 Central Pacific cyclone") formed on October 30, 2006 in the central Pacific subtropics. It eventually developed an [eye-like](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_(cyclone) "Eye (cyclone)") structure.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-NASA-91C-113) Its track data indicates that it crossed from the central to the east Pacific because it formed at longitude 149°W and dissipated at 135°W.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Padgett_tracks-114)[NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA"), which is not a meteorological organization, called this system a [subtropical cyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_cyclone "Subtropical cyclone"), and the Naval Research Laboratory Monterey had enough interest in it to call it 91C.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-NASA-91C-113) The system has also been called [extratropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extratropical_cyclone "Extratropical cyclone").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CHC-115) This cyclone is unofficial because it is not included in the seasonal reports of either [Regional Specialized Meteorological Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Specialized_Meteorological_Center "Regional Specialized Meteorological Center").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CPHC_2006-116)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-NHC_2006_archive-117)

### California

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: California")]

See also: [List of California hurricanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_California_hurricanes "List of California hurricanes")

*   **After October or before June, 1854**– A system considered a tropical cyclone makes landfall just north of the [Golden Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate "Golden Gate").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Visher_p296-88)
*   **October 2, 1858**– A [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1858_San_Diego_hurricane "1858 San Diego hurricane") makes a direct hit on Southern California before dissipating. The hurricane may or may not have made landfall in [San Diego County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_County,_California "San Diego County, California"), due to uncertainty in the track reconstruction. [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego") experienced hurricane-force winds, with torrential rainfall recorded all across Southern California.
*   **After October or before June, 1859**– A system considered a tropical cyclone makes landfall between [Cape Mendocino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Mendocino "Cape Mendocino") and [San Francisco Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay "San Francisco Bay").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Visher_p296-88)
*   **September 25, 1939**– The [1939 California tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_California_tropical_storm "1939 California tropical storm") makes landfall in [San Pedro, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Pedro,_California "San Pedro, California"), killing 45[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Hurd_1939-124) to 93 people.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-history_of_sig_events_p14-125)
*   **September 6, 1972**– [Tropical Depression Hyacinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Pacific_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Hyacinth "1972 Pacific hurricane season") makes landfall.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_Hyacinth_1972-126)
*   **September 6, 1978**– [Tropical Depression Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Norman_(1978) "Hurricane Norman (1978)") makes landfall.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_Norman_1978-127)

This is a **list of notable Pacific hurricanes**, subdivided by reason for notability. Notability means that it has met some criterion or achieved some statistic, or is part of a top ten for some superlative. It includes lists and rankings of [Pacific hurricanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_hurricane "Pacific hurricane") by different characteristics and impacts.

Characteristics include extremes of location, such as the northernmost or most equator-ward formation or position of a tropical cyclone. Other characteristics include its central pressure, windspeed, category on the [Saffir–Simpson scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saffir%E2%80%93Simpson_scale "Saffir–Simpson scale"), [cyclogenesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclogenesis "Tropical cyclogenesis") outside of a normal [hurricane season's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_hurricane "Pacific hurricane") timeframe, or storms that remain unnamed despite forming after tropical cyclone naming began in 1960. Another characteristic is how long a system lasted from formation to dissipation. These include the cost of damage, the number of casualties, as well as meteorological statistics such as rainfall point maximum, wind speed, and minimum pressure.

### Retired names

Main article: [List of retired Pacific hurricane names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_retired_Pacific_hurricane_names "List of retired Pacific hurricane names")

The following names have been retired in the East Pacific (in chronological order): [Hazel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Hazel_(1965) "Tropical Storm Hazel (1965)"), [Adele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Adele_(1970) "Hurricane Adele (1970)"), [Fico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fico "Hurricane Fico"), [Knut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Knut_(1987) "Tropical Storm Knut (1987)"), [Iva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iva_(1988) "Hurricane Iva (1988)"), [Fefa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Fefa "Hurricane Fefa"), [Ismael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ismael "Hurricane Ismael"), [Pauline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Pauline "Hurricane Pauline"), [Adolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Adolph_(2001) "Hurricane Adolph (2001)"), Israel, [Kenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Kenna "Hurricane Kenna"), [Alma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Alma "Tropical Storm Alma"), [Manuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Manuel "Hurricane Manuel"), [Odile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Odile "Hurricane Odile"), Isis, [Patricia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Patricia "Hurricane Patricia"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HRD-1)[Dora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Dora_(2023) "Hurricane Dora (2023)"), [Otis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Otis "Hurricane Otis"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-WMO24-2) and [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_John_(2024) "Hurricane John (2024)").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-WMO25-3)

In addition, the following names have been retired in the Central Pacific (in chronological order): [Iwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iwa "Hurricane Iwa"), [Iniki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iniki "Hurricane Iniki"), [Paka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoon_Paka "Typhoon Paka"), and [Ioke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ioke "Hurricane Ioke").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HRD-1)

A few years later, the [Dvorak technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvorak_technique "Dvorak technique") came into use. Those two factors make intensity estimates more reliable starting in that year.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Padgett_August_2000-44) For these reasons, seasons prior to 1971 are not included.

### Naming history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Naming history")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Oho_2015-10-06_2310Z.jpg/250px-Oho_2015-10-06_2310Z.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Oho_2015-10-06_2310Z.jpg)

[Hurricane Oho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Oho "Hurricane Oho"), the eighth system to receive a central Pacific name in 2015

Naming of tropical cyclones in the eastern north Pacific began in the [1960 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_Pacific_hurricane_season "1960 Pacific hurricane season"). That year, four lists of names were created. The plan was to proceed in a manner similar to that of the western Pacific; that is, the name of the first storm in one season would be the next unused one from the same list, and when the bottom of one list was reached the next list was started. This scheme was abandoned in 1965 and next year, the lists started being recycled on a four-year rotation, starting with the A name each year.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-ATWC-51) That same general scheme remains in use today, although the names and lists are different. On average, the eastern north Pacific sees about sixteen named storms per year.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-NCDC_2006_summary-52)

The geostationary satellite era began in 1966,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Rhome_Brown_Mainelli_Blake-43) and that year is often considered the first year of reliable tropical records.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Padgett_August_2000-44) Intensity estimates are more reliable starting in the 1971 season. A few years later, the [Dvorak technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dvorak_technique "Dvorak technique") came into use. Those two make intensity estimates more reliable starting in that year.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Padgett_August_2000-44) For these reasons, seasons before 1971 are not included in the "Fewest named" column.

## Duration records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Duration records")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Tina_1992-09-30_1801Z.png/250px-Tina_1992-09-30_1801Z.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tina_1992-09-30_1801Z.png)

[Hurricane Tina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Tina_(1992) "Hurricane Tina (1992)"), the longest-lasting Pacific hurricane east of the International Date Line

This lists all Pacific hurricanes that existed as tropical cyclones while in the Pacific Ocean east of [the dateline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/180th_meridian "180th meridian") for more than two weeks continuously. Hurricanes John and Dora spent some time in the west Pacific before dissipating. John spent eleven days west of the dateline; if that time was included John would have existed for a total of 30 days and 18 hours, while including Dora's time in the west Pacific would mean that it existed for 18 days.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53) One Atlantic hurricane, [Hurricane Joan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Joan%E2%80%93Miriam "Hurricane Joan–Miriam"), crossed into this basin and was renamed Miriam,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-E15-69) giving it a total lifespan of 22 days,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-HURDAT-70) but not all of that was in the Pacific. 1993's Greg formed from the remnants of [Tropical Storm Bret (1993)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Bret_(1993) "Tropical Storm Bret (1993)").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-E15-69) Its time as an Atlantic system is excluded.

All of these systems except Trudy, Olaf, Connie and Lala existed in both the east and central Pacific, and all except Olaf were hurricanes. Hurricane Trudy of 1990 is thus the longest lived eastern Pacific hurricane to stay in the eastern Pacific. Tropical Storm Olaf of 1997 is hence the longest-lived eastern Pacific tropical cyclone _not_ to reach hurricane intensity.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53)

Prior to [Hurricane Lala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Lala "Hurricane Lala")[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_], no known tropical cyclone forming in the central north Pacific lasted for longer than 14 days without crossing into [another basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone_basins "Tropical cyclone basins").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-EPAC_HURDAT-53) The pre-2026 tropical cyclone that formed in the central Pacific and spent the most time there was [Hurricane Ana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ana "Hurricane Ana"), at 12.75 days from formation to extratropical transition.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-AnaTCR-71)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-tc_records_CPHC-72)

It used to be that when a Pacific named storm crossed North America and made it to the Atlantic (or vice versa), it would receive the next name on the respective basin's list. However, in 2000 this policy was changed so that a tropical cyclone will keep its name if it remains a tropical cyclone during the entire passage. Only if it dissipates and then re-forms does it get renamed.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-b5-87)

## Unusual landfall locations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Unusual landfall locations")]

### California

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: California")]

See also: [List of California hurricanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_California_hurricanes "List of California hurricanes")

*   **After October or before June, 1854**– A system considered a tropical cyclone makes landfall just north of the [Golden Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gate "Golden Gate").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Visher_p296-88)
*   **October 2, 1858**– A [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1858_San_Diego_hurricane "1858 San Diego hurricane") makes a direct hit on Southern California before dissipating. The hurricane may or may not have made landfall in [San Diego County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_County,_California "San Diego County, California"), due to uncertainty in the track reconstruction. [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego") experienced hurricane-force winds, with torrential rainfall recorded all across Southern California.
*   **After October or before June, 1859**– A system considered a tropical cyclone makes landfall between [Cape Mendocino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Mendocino "Cape Mendocino") and [San Francisco Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay "San Francisco Bay").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Visher_p296-88)
*   **September 25, 1939**– The [1939 California tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_California_tropical_storm "1939 California tropical storm") makes landfall in [San Pedro, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Pedro,_California "San Pedro, California"), killing 45[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Hurd_1939-124) to 93 people.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-history_of_sig_events_p14-125)
*   **September 6, 1972**– [Tropical Depression Hyacinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Pacific_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Hyacinth "1972 Pacific hurricane season") makes landfall.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_Hyacinth_1972-126)
*   **September 6, 1978**– [Tropical Depression Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Norman_(1978) "Hurricane Norman (1978)") makes landfall.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_Norman_1978-127)

*   **September 14, 1992**– [Tropical Depression Orlene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Pacific_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Orlene "1992 Pacific hurricane season") makes landfall on the Big Island.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CPHC_1992-64)
*   **July 24, 1993**– [Tropical Depression Eugene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Eugene_(1993) "Hurricane Eugene (1993)") makes landfall on the [Big Island of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Island_of_Hawaii "Big Island of Hawaii").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Unisys_EUGENE_1993-132)
*   **August 8, 2014**– [Tropical Storm Iselle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Iselle_(2014) "Hurricane Iselle (2014)") makes landfall on the [Big Island of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Island_of_Hawaii "Big Island of Hawaii"), killing one on [Kauai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kauai "Kauai").[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Fox_News-133)
*   **July 24, 2016**– [Tropical Storm Darby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Darby_(2016) "Hurricane Darby (2016)") makes landfall on the [Big Island of Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Island_of_Hawaii "Big Island of Hawaii").[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-Al_Jazeera-134)
*   **September 12, 2018**– [Tropical Storm Olivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Olivia_(2018) "Hurricane Olivia (2018)") makes landfall on [Maui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui "Maui") and [Lanai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanai "Lanai").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records#cite_note-CNN-135)

I was unable to produce the requested counts because the raw best‑track data (NOAA HURDAT2) is available as a large plain‑text file (e.g., `hurdat2-nepac-1949-2024-031725.txt` – https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/hurdat/hurdat2-nepac-1949-2024-031725.txt) but no pre‑compiled, decade‑resolved summary of “hurricanes that were within 60 nm of the Mexican coast” exists on the web, and the text file must be parsed and filtered to generate the figures.  No source provides a ready‑made list of:

* the number of Pacific hurricanes that originated off the west coast of Mexico per decade (1990‑1999, 2000‑2009, 2010‑2019),  
* the number of Atlantic hurricanes that originated off the east (Gulf) coast of Mexico per decade,  
* the difference between those numbers for each decade, or  
* a list of Category 4 storms that came within 60 nm of either coast during the decade with the largest difference.

Sources that confirm the availability of the raw data but do not contain the derived counts:

* NOAA HURDAT2 NE/NC Pacific‐Basin file (contains track points for every storm in the eastern Pacific): https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/hurdat/hurdat2-nepac-1949-2024-031725.txt (Reference: “EP011949 … 7 … 1949‐06‐11 … 20.2N 106.3W 45 …” as shown in the file).  
* NOAA data index page listing the HURDAT files: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/hurdat/  
* Wikipedia “List of Pacific hurricane records” (mentions NOAA HURDAT2 but no decade‑by‑decade counts): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pacific_hurricane_records.

Because the necessary aggregated counts and the list of Category 4 storms have not been extracted or published in a source I could access, I cannot identify which decade has the largest difference between west‑ and east‑coast origins, nor can I provide the alphabetic list of Category 4 hurricanes within 60 nm of either coast for that decade.
